To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HRM function is not well suited to support self‐managing teams.

(1) the use of self-managing teams in the workplace has a positive impact on organizational effectiveness; and (2) self-managing team effectiveness is positively influenced by team autonomy, team support, team member skills, and team member commitment to the organization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the human resource professional in the context of self‐managining work teams.
how self‐management can be used to enhance the performance of the team.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HRM professional has to be more involved in the process of team formation and development, and has to be more proactive and flexible in the application of HRM policies and programmes.
self‐managing teams are not a panacea for all of the ills in organizations.
the human resources department must be involved with the implementation of self‐managed work teams.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self‐management of work teams is a new and promising organizational form that can be successfully used in a wide variety of organizational situations.
we have shown that the use of self‐manag ing work teams can be effective in improving performance and that this effectiveness is enhanced when the HRM process is modified to support the team.
the use of Self-Managing Work Teams (SMTs) has been shown to be a viable approach to managing work.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SMWTs can be a very effective way to increase productivity and reduce costs.
the benefits of SMWT are contingent on a number of factors.
the HRM function should not be seen as a separate entity from the rest of the organization.
